summary.why: This party says that too large a share of NZ health spending goes towards caring for people once they're sick, as opposed to before. statement: Increase sentence lengths for murder

summary.why: This party says that the criminal justice system needs to prioritise victims over perpetrators. Part of this, the party argues, requires longer sentences for violent and sexual offences. The party is concerned that those on trial for murder can have their sentences reduced because of technicalities. It says a formal degree of murder regime needs to be introduced to counteract this.
summary.how: This party would introduce a formal degree of murder regime whereby first degree murder is life imprisonment without a chance of parole; second degree murder is an aggravated life sentence with a minimum sentence of non-parole period of 30 years. Third degree murder would be a life sentence with a minimum non-parole period of 10 years. The party would also increase sentences for attempted murder and wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm from 14 years to 25 years. It would increase the standard parole eligibility to 75% of a sentence for long-term offenders so that those convicted of murder have to be assessed as having a low probability of reoffending before release. It would also limit sentence discounts for factors other than a guilty plea to 10%. Guilty plea discounts will remain limited to 25%.

statement: Expand self-defence justifications in the justice system

summary.why: This party says that the criminal justice system should prioritise victims as opposed to offenders. A component of better serving victims, the party says, is ensuring trusted and effective self-defence protections and recognising home burglaries as aggravated due to the impact of such offences on people, not just property.
summary.how: This party would investigate the best practice to establish 'stand your ground' laws for when someone has committed violence while defending their person and their property. It would amend Police operational and prosecution guidelines to make it clear that a person who excessively defends themselves is to be treated initially as a victim unless evidence indicates otherwise. The Solicitor-General’s prosecution guidelines would be amended so more weight is given to juries. Additionally, the Solicitor-General would be required to approve that any prosecution based on self-defence is in the public interest. Additionally, the party would ensure that home burglaries are regarded as aggravated.
